title: Apollo’s Slok says US companies now treat AI spending as a cost, not growth
excerpt: ‘Mainstream corporate America is pulling back,’ says Apollo’s Torsten Slok, finding no AI payoff in revenue or margins outside tech.
content_html:
Artificial intelligence has delivered “zero financial payoff” to corporate America outside the tech sector. That is the finding of Torsten Slok, chief economist at Apollo Global Management, in a note on Saturday.

Slok compared the Magnificent Seven, the biggest US tech companies, with the other 493 companies in the S&P 500. Revenue per worker and profit margins are rising for the first group and flat for the second, he wrote. He also found no sign yet of AI lifting productivity growth.

“Mainstream corporate America is pulling back and starting to view token spending not as a source of growth but as a cost center that weighs on margins.” Torsten Slok, Apollo Global Management

Business Insider read the charts for the numbers. Revenue per employee at the tech giants rose from about $550,000 in 2022 to nearly $800,000. The rest of the S&P 500 stayed near $550,000, with profit margins at about 10%.

Who is paying for tokens

Tokens are the units AI companies charge by. Venture-backed companies are spending more and more on them, Slok wrote. Mainstream companies, he added, do not need the latest model and are unwilling to pay for it.

Apollo’s charts use data from the spending platform Ramp. They show the top 10% of firms account for 95.6% of spending on OpenAI and Anthropic. Venture capital backs most of the top 1% of AI spenders. Some large employers are already capping use: Accenture this month limited staff Claude spending to $29 a month.

“As long as agentic AI and token spending are confined to a small part of the economy, the macroeconomic effects of AI will be very limited.” Torsten Slok

Slok made a related case on 20 October. Corporate token spending is growing more slowly, he wrote in an earlier note. That suggests demand for compute may exist “only when compute is effectively free”. In August, Apollo found AI was hitting paychecks rather than payrolls.

A week of Big Tech results

Not everyone on Wall Street shares the view. Blackstone president Jon Gray last week rejected warnings of an AI bubble and called demand “almost parabolic”, Bloomberg reported. He was speaking about an AI consulting business Blackstone set up with Anthropic.

Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft report quarterly earnings this week, with investors looking for an AI payoff from their spending. Earlier this month, Gartner warned that $3.5tn of AI infrastructure spending could face write-downs by 2030.

“[T]he AI story will be decided in the S&P 493, not the Mag 7.” Torsten Slok
